se_hero_title_lead: Work, time, money and everyday life.
se_hero_lead: Self-Engine is my own product: a productivity app for freelancers and the self-employed in which time tracking, tasks, calendar, finance and habits share one data model. I design, build and run it on my own — offline-first, on the web, on the Mac and soon on your phone.
cs_flow_heading: Separate tools know nothing about each other.
cs_flow_p1: Time trackers don't know what an hour is worth. Finance apps don't know which work earned the money. And calendars show what was planned — never what actually happened. The connections between them only existed in my head.
cs_flow_p2: In Self-Engine, those connections are the product: an appointment starts a timer, the timer becomes a time entry, and a payout marks the entries as paid and books the money in Finance.
cs_flow_step_5_sub: in the right account and currency
cs_flow_note: And habits fill themselves in — from the time you track on a linked project.
cs_mod_lead: Each module works on its own — and knows about the others.

cs_ai_p1: The built-in assistant knows 39 typed capabilities across every module. It works pull-first: the model gets counts and hints instead of user data and has to ask through typed read tools. The server enforces rate limits, cost tracking and routing through zero-data-retention endpoints only.
cs_ai_p2: If you'd rather use your own agent, connect Claude, Claude Code or Cursor to Self-Engine's MCP server over OAuth. Permissions apply per data type, agents can at most move things to the trash, and every call lands in the agent log.
cs_ai_step_2_body: once, bound to the exact input
cs_ai_step_3_body: the same domain mutation as a click
cs_arch_p1: Every app writes to a local SQLite database first; a write never waits for the cloud. PowerSync queues the change and uploads it in order to Supabase, where Postgres, with row-level security on every table, stays the source of truth. Changes from other devices flow back into the local database, and the UI updates through live queries — no manual cache invalidation anywhere.
cs_arch_p2: The domain lives in shared packages: 37 synced tables, Zod schemas and typed collections that web and mobile consume identically. Business rules are pure functions behind a persistence port — the same rule guards a tap in the mobile app, a click on the web and an AI agent's tool call on the server.
cs_arch_p3: Identity is a single Clerk JWT for both data paths: PowerSync validates it for replication, and Postgres enforces it through row-level security on every query. The desktop app is an Electron shell around the web app — with a menu-bar timer, quick capture and signed auto-updates.
cs_diagram_port: Persistence port: the same business rules on the device, on the server and in tests
cs_learn1_body: So that AI agents on the server hit the same rules as the app on the device, I pulled the domain logic off PowerSync and behind a persistence port — with three adapters (PowerSync, in-memory, Postgres) and a test that checks every rule's import graph.
cs_learn2_title: One broken write must not block the rest
cs_learn2_body: Offline queues upload in strict order — a single invalid write would hold up every one after it. So fatal Postgres errors are classified and dropped, writes that belong together are sent atomically, and you learn which area lost a change.
cs_learn3_title: Calendar sync on an offline foundation
cs_learn3_body: The hard part of syncing with Google and iCloud isn't the API, it's identity: deterministic IDs make creates idempotent, ETags catch concurrent edits, expired sync tokens trigger a full resync, and the server-side reconciliation shares a lock with the sync from the app.
cs_learn4_title: Swapping the identity provider in production
cs_learn4_body: Migrating every user ID from Supabase Auth to Clerk meant rewriting every row-level security policy in one migration and moving two independent data paths to one JWT — without losing a single offline queue.
cs_cta_body: Self-Engine runs in the browser and on the Mac — free for 30 days.
cs_cta_note: Self-Engine is a commercial product; its source code is not public.
